knowledge_fragments.content: Opposite to NBTE, infective endocarditis usually manifests with fever and chills, with possible septic signs. Also, (subacute) infective endocarditis can be associated with the presence of micro-embolic phenomena such as retinal Roth spots; splinter and conjunctival hemorrhages; and immunologic manifestations presenting with vasculitic cutaneous lesions, namely, the Osler’s nodules and Janeway’s lesions. Metastatic infection is also common in cases of infective endocarditis, particularly with peripheral abscesses, mycotic aneurysms, and spondylodiscitis.

knowledge_fragments.content: Presentation: A 55-year-old Japanese woman with no significant medical history presented with a two-month history of malaise and myalgia, and a one-month history of fever. She had no relevant history regarding pets, travel, dental treatment, or drug abuse. She worked at an import grocery store. Physical examination revealed a body temperature of 37.6°C, a grade 2 systolic murmur at the apex, and a painful 1 mm black induration on her right forefinger. Laboratory tests showed a white blood cell count of 8200/μL, a C-reactive protein level of 6.6 mg/dL, and a hemoglobin level of 9.9 g/dL.. knowledge_fragments.content: Presentation: A 61-year-old man presented with intermittent fever and malaise for 4 months. Initially, he experienced a fever reaching up to 40°C, mostly in the afternoon and at night, accompanied by chills and malaise. After 3 days of self-administered anti-infection treatment, his body temperature normalized, but the fever recurred upon cessation of the treatment. The condition progressively worsened, leading to decreased blood pressure and an increased heart rate. The patient was diagnosed with infectious shock and transferred for further treatment. He had no prior health issues or family history of disease. Physical examination showed slightly pale skin and mucous membranes, no jugular vein enlargement, but an enlarged cardiac border to the left. A grade III-IV diastolic murmur was noted in the aortic valve area, along with positive peripheral vascular signs. Laboratory tests indicated normal leukocyte and neutrophil counts, C-reactive protein at 53.1 mg/L, calcitonin at 2.66 ng/mL, and normal liver and renal function tests. knowledge_fragments.content: Cardiac masses are a broad set of space-occupying structures within the cardiac cavities or adjacent to the pericardium that remain a common diagnostic challenge in cardiology practice and can be broadly classified as neoplastic or non-neoplastic. The latter include frequently diagnosed clinical entities such as thrombi and vegetations, while neoplastic masses are comprised of metastases from extracardiac tumors and primary cardiac tumors (PCTs), both benign and malignant. Secondary metastases are by far the most frequent form of cardiac tumors and, by definition, malignant. PCTs, on the contrary, are exceedingly rare and mostly benign (90%). In adults, the most common histotypes of benign cardiac tumors include myxomas, lipomas, and papillary fibroelastomas (PFEs), while in the pediatric population rhabdomyomas and fibromas are by far more represented. On the other hand, primary malignant cardiac tumors (such as sarcoma, angiosarcoma, rhabdomyoma, and lymphoma) are rare. The clinical presentation of cardiac tumors can be heterogeneous. The incubation period averages 18 to 21 days (range 9 to 28 days). Some infections are minimally

symptomatic; however, most patients have influenza-like symptoms. Onset is abrupt, with fever, severe

headache, chills, severe malaise, myalgia, anorexia, and sweats. Fever may rise to 40° C and persist 1 to

> 3 wk. Respiratory symptoms (a dry nonproductive cough, pleuritic chest pain) appear 4 to 5 days after

onset of illness. These symptoms may be particularly severe in elderly or debilitated patients. During

examination, lung crackles are commonly noted, and findings suggesting consolidation may be present.

Unlike rickettsial diseases, acute Q fever does not cause a rash.

Acute hepatic involvement, occurring in some patients, resembles viral hepatitis, with fever, malaise,

hepatomegaly with right upper abdominal pain, and possibly jaundice. Headache and respiratory signs

are frequently absent. Chronic Q fever hepatitis may manifest as FUO. Liver biopsy may show

granulomas, which should be differentiated from other causes of liver granulomas (eg, TB, sarcoidosis,

histoplasmosis, brucellosis, tularemia, syphilis).

the nature of the murmur
family history
age (especially if over 75),
or
medical history (for example, a history of atrial fibrillation).

knowledge_fragments.content:
Symptoms vary. Subclavian aneurysms can cause local pain, a pulsating sensation, venous thrombosis or

edema (due to compression of adjacent veins), distal ischemic symptoms,

transient ischemic attacks,

stroke, or hoarseness or impaired motor and sensory function (due to compression of the recurrent

laryngeal nerve or brachial plexus). Superior mesenteric aneurysms may cause abdominal pain and

ischemic colitis.

Regardless of location, mycotic or inflammatory aneurysms may cause local pain and sequelae of

systemic infection (eg, fever, malaise, weight loss).

knowledge_fragments.content: Presentation: An 8-month-old child was referred for evaluation of a cardiac murmur. The child showed no symptoms and exhibited normal growth patterns without signs of congestive heart failure. General examination indicated the child was afebrile, with no pallor, cyanosis, or clubbing, and normal jugular venous pressure. Vital signs were stable. Physical examination identified a 4/6 harsh systolic murmur at the right upper sternal border. Other system examinations were unremarkable. Chest X-ray results were normal, and the electrocardiogram revealed sinus tachycardia.. Confirmed diagnosis: Unicuspid Aortic Valve. Differential diagnosis includes: Unicuspid Aortic Valve.

Pyoderma gangrenosum begins as an inflamed erythematous papule, pustule, or nodule. The lesion,

which may resemble a furuncle or an arthropod bite at this stage, then ulcerates and expands rapidly,

developing a swollen necrotic base and a raised dusky to violaceous border. An undermined border is

common, if not pathognomonic. Systemic symptoms such as fever, malaise, and arthralgias are common.

knowledge_fragments.content: Presentation: A 7-year-old boy was brought to the cardiology outpatient clinic due to a cardiac murmur. His family history was unremarkable, and his own health had been normal until he started school 2 years prior. Since then, his parents noticed he had less exercise tolerance compared to other children his age. On physical examination, the boy appeared well-nourished. His blood pressure and transcutaneous oxygen saturation (SaO2) were within normal limits. The examination revealed a hyperactive precordium, an intense second heart sound, and a diastolic murmur over the pulmonary artery. There were no signs of heart failure. Lung sounds were normal, and the liver was not enlarged. Electrocardiography (ECG) indicated right ventricular hypertrophy.. Confirmed diagnosis: Idiopathic Pulmonary Arterial Hypertension. Differential diagnosis includes: Idiopathic Pulmonary Arterial Hypertension.
knowledge_fragments.title: Case report: Idiopathic Pulmonary Arterial Hypertension

knowledge_fragments.content:
Many cases are mild. After a 14- to 21-day incubation period, a 1- to 5-day prodrome, usually consisting

of low-grade fever, malaise, and lymphadenopathy, occurs in adults but may be minimal or absent in

children. Tender swelling of the suboccipital, postauricular, and posterior cervical glands is characteristic.

There is pharyngeal injection at the onset.

The rash is similar to that of measles but is less extensive and more evanescent (see

Plate 64

); it is often the first sign in children. It begins on the face and neck and quickly spreads to the

trunk and extremities. At onset, a blanching, macular erythema may appear, particularly on the face. On

the 2nd day, the rash often becomes more scarlatiniform (pinpoint) with a reddish flush. Petechiae form on

the soft palate (Forschheimer's spots), later coalescing into a red blush. The rash lasts 3 to 5 days.

Constitutional symptoms in children are absent or mild and may include malaise and occasional

arthralgias. Adults usually have few or no constitutional symptoms but occasionally have fever, malaise,

headache, stiff joints, transient arthritis, and mild rhinitis. Fever typically resolves by the 2nd day of the

rash.

knowledge_fragments.content: Presentation: A 2-day-old female infant was assessed at Chonnam National University Hospital due to the presence of a cardiac murmur. She was delivered via Caesarean section at a local hospital, with a birth weight of 3.4 kg. Antenatal ultrasonography had indicated a potential ventricular septal defect. Physical examination revealed a grade 1 systolic murmur located at the left lower sternal border, with no other notable findings.. Confirmed diagnosis: Partial anomalous pulmonary venous connection. Differential diagnosis includes: Partial anomalous pulmonary venous connection.

knowledge_fragments.content: Symptoms of infection with the virus begin with mild headache followed by a maculopapular rash (neck, face, trunk, and upper arms, and spread to palms and soles), fever, malaise, conjunctivitis, and joint pains. It also causes microcephaly in newborn babies through mother-to-child transmission and neurologic conditions in infected adults, including Guillain-Barré syndrome.

Chest x-ray abnormalities include bibasilar hazy opacities without honeycombing; findings may be normal

in up to 20% of cases. HRCT shows multifocal or diffuse, basilar, subpleural ground-glass opacities.

Irregular linear and reticular opacities are common but are not usually the dominant features.

knowledge_fragments.content: Presentation: A 36-year-old male presented with shortness of breath and swelling in the lower extremities for the past 2 weeks. The patient also reported experiencing intermittent fever over the last 2 months. Upon admission, vital signs included a heart rate of 103 beats per minute, blood pressure of 122/47 mmHg, and a temperature of 37.2°C. Cardiac examination identified a pandiastolic murmur in the aortic region. Laboratory tests indicated an elevated NT-proBNP level of 4492.0 pg/mL. Transthoracic echocardiography demonstrated bicuspid aortic valve and severe aortic regurgitation (AR) secondary to vegetations and prolapse of aortic valve. Subsequent blood culture grew Streptococcus gordonii.. Confirmed diagnosis: Subacute Bacterial Endocarditis. Differential diagnosis includes: Subacute Bacterial Endocarditis.

knowledge_fragments.content:
The symptoms and signs are similar for all ETBR and generally milder than with spotted fever. After an

incubation period of 5 to 7 days, fever, malaise, headache, and conjunctival injection develop. With the

onset of fever, a small buttonlike ulcer 2 to 5 mm in diameter with a black center appears (an eschar or, in

boutonneuse fever, tache noire). Usually, the regional or satellite lymph nodes are enlarged. On about the

4th day of fever, a red maculopapular rash appears on the forearms and extends to most of the body,

including the palms and soles. Fever lasts into the 2nd wk.

Complications and death are rare except among elderly or debilitated patients. However, the disease

should not be ignored; a fulminant form of vasculitis can occur.

Patients commonly have acute diarrhea with fever and malaise. A chronic phase of milder diarrhea,

nausea, anorexia, abdominal cramps, and fatigue follows. Steatorrhea is common. Nutritional

deficiencies, especially of folate and vitamin B

, eventually develop after several months to years. The

patient may also have weight loss, glossitis, stomatitis, and peripheral edema.

tree.case_summary:
A 65-year-old man presents with four months of low-grade fever and malaise. He also says he has lost 9 kg (20 lb) during this period and suffers from extreme fatigue. Past medical history is significant for a mitral valve replacement five years ago. His temperature is 38.1°C (100.6°F), respirations are 22/min, pulse is 102/min, and blood pressure is 138/78 mm Hg. On physical examination, there is a new onset 2/6 holosystolic murmur, loudest in the apical area of the precordium. Which of the following organisms is the most likely cause of this patient’s condition?

Options:
A. *Pseudomonas aeruginosa*
B. *Bartonella henselae*
C. HACEK group organisms
D. *Candida albicans*
E. Beta-hemolytic streptococci
F. *Staphylococcus aureus*
G. Coagulase-negative *Staphylococcus spp.*
H. *Pseudomonas* aeruginosa
I. *Streptococcus bovis*
J. *Enterococcus*

excluded_candidates: Infective endocarditis: possible but requires further evidence
Chronic infection: unlikely given the subacute presentation
